1. What is badness? It is what you have often seen. And whenever anything happens, keep this in mind: it is what you have often seen. Wherever you look, high and low, you will find the same things. The old histories are full of them, and so are the histories of the middle ages and of our own day; cities and houses are full of them now. There is nothing new. Everything is both familiar and short-lived.

2. How can our principles die, unless the impressions—the thoughts—that go with them are put out? But it is in your power to keep fanning these thoughts into a flame. I can hold the opinion I ought to hold about anything. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind have nothing at all to do with my mind. Let this be your state of mind, and you stand upright. It is in your power to get your life back. Look at things again as you used to look at them; that is what getting your life back means.

3. The empty business of putting on a show, plays on the stage, flocks of sheep, herds, drills with spears, a bone thrown to puppies, a crumb of bread tossed into a fishpond, ants toiling and carrying their loads, frightened little mice scurrying here and there, puppets jerked on strings—it is all alike. Your duty, then, in the middle of all this is to show good humor, not a haughty air. But understand, too, that each person is worth exactly as much as the things he busies himself with.

4. In conversation you must pay attention to what is being said, and in every impulse you must watch what is being done. In the one, see at once what end it is aimed at; in the other, watch carefully what is meant.

5. Is my understanding equal to this task or not? If it is, I use it for the work as a tool given to me by the nature of the universe. If it is not, then either I step back from the work and give way to someone who can do it better—unless there is some reason why I ought not to—or I do it as well as I can, taking as my helper someone who, with the support of my ruling faculty, can do what the moment calls for and what is useful for the common good. For whatever I can do, by myself or with someone else, ought to aim at one thing only: what is useful to the community and fitting for it.
6. How many who were once celebrated and famous have been handed over to oblivion; and how many of those who celebrated the fame of others are long since dead.

7. Do not be ashamed to be helped. Your task is to do your duty, like a soldier storming a city wall. What if you are lame and cannot climb onto the battlements alone, but can with someone else's help?
8. Do not let the future disturb you. You will come to it, if you have to, carrying the same reason that you now use for the present.

9. All things are woven together, and the bond between them is holy; hardly anything is unconnected with anything else. For things have been set in order together, and together they make up one and the same ordered universe. For there is one universe made up of all things, and one god who pervades all things, and one substance, and one law, one reason shared by all intelligent beings, and one truth—if indeed there is also one perfection for all beings who are of the same stock and share in the same reason.

10. Everything material soon vanishes into the substance of the whole. Everything that is form and cause is very soon taken back into the reason that governs the universe. And the memory of everything is very soon buried under time.
11. For a rational being, the same act is in keeping with nature and in keeping with reason.
12. Stand upright, or be set upright.

13. What the limbs are in a single body, rational beings are to one another, even though they exist apart; for they have been made to work together as one. You will see this more clearly if you often say to yourself: "I am a limb (melos) of the body that rational beings make up." But if you change one letter to r and say that you are merely a part (meros), you do not yet love people from your heart. Doing good does not yet delight you for its own sake. You still do it simply because it is the proper thing to do, and not yet as a good done to yourself.

14. Let whatever will fall from outside fall on the parts that can feel it. Those parts that have felt it can complain, if they like. But I am not harmed unless I judge that what has happened is bad. And it is in my power not to judge so.
15. Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good—just as if gold, or emerald, or purple were always saying: "Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and keep my color."

16. The ruling faculty does not disturb itself; I mean, it does not frighten itself or bring pain on itself. If someone else can frighten it or cause it pain, let him. It will not turn itself that way by its own judgment. Let the body take care, if it can, that it suffers nothing; and if it suffers, let it say so. But the soul itself—the part that feels fear and pain, and that has full power to form an opinion about them—will suffer nothing, for it will never turn aside into such a judgment. The ruling faculty, in itself, needs nothing, unless it creates a need for itself. And so it is free from disturbance and free from hindrance, provided it does not disturb or hinder itself.

17. Happiness—eudaemonia—means a good divine spirit, or a good thing. So what are you doing here, imagination? Go away, I beg you by the gods, the way you came. I do not want you. But you have come in your old way. I am not angry with you; only go away.

18. Is anyone afraid of change? But what can come about without change? What is dearer or more fitting to the nature of the universe? Can you take a bath unless the wood that heats it is changed? Can you be fed unless your food is changed? Can anything else that is useful be done without change? Do you not see, then, that your own change is just the same, and just as necessary to the nature of the universe?

19. All bodies are carried through the substance of the universe as through a rushing torrent. By their nature they are united with the whole and work together with it, as the parts of our body work together with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has time already swallowed up! Let the same thought come to you about every person and every thing.
20. Only one thing troubles me: that I may do something the constitution of a human being does not allow, or do it in a way it does not allow, or do what it does not allow at this moment.
21. Soon you will have forgotten everything; and soon everyone will have forgotten you.

22. It is a human being's own mark to love even those who do wrong. And this happens if, when they do wrong, it occurs to you that they are your kin; that they do wrong out of ignorance and without meaning to; that soon both of you will be dead; and above all, that the wrongdoer has done you no harm, for he has not made your ruling faculty worse than it was before.

23. The nature of the universe works the substance of the universe as if it were wax. Now it shapes a horse; then it breaks the horse up and uses the material for a tree, then for a human being, then for something else. And each of these things lasts for a very short time. But it is no hardship for a container to be broken up, just as it was none for it to be put together.

24. A scowling face is entirely against nature. When it is put on often, all beauty dies out of the face, and at last is put out so completely that it can never be lit again. Try to conclude from this very fact that scowling is against reason. For if even the awareness of doing wrong is lost, what reason is left for living any longer?

25. The nature that governs the whole will soon change everything you see. Out of their substance it will make other things, and out of the substance of those, still others, so that the world may always be new.

26. When someone wrongs you, consider at once what opinion about good or bad led him to do it. Once you see this, you will pity him, and you will be neither surprised nor angry. For either you yourself think the same thing is good as he does, or something of the same kind. So it is your duty to forgive him. But if you do not think such things are good or bad, you will find it easier to feel goodwill toward someone who has gone astray.

27. Do not think so much about what you do not have as about what you have. Of the things you have, pick out the best, and then consider how eagerly you would have longed for them if you did not have them. At the same time, though, be careful not to become so pleased with them that you grow used to overvaluing them, so that you would be upset if you ever lost them.
28. Withdraw into yourself. It is the nature of your rational ruling faculty to be content with itself when it acts justly, and in that way to keep its calm.

29. Wipe out the impression. Stop the jerking of the strings. Keep yourself to the present. Understand clearly what is happening, whether to you or to someone else. Divide every object and sort it into what is its cause—its form—and what is its matter. Think of your last hour. Let the wrong someone has done stay where the wrong was done.
30. Pay attention to what is said. Let your mind go right into the things that are being done and into the things that do them.

31. Clothe yourself in simplicity and modesty, and in indifference toward the things that lie between virtue and vice. Love humankind. Follow God. The poet says that law rules all—and it is enough to remember that law rules all.
32. On death: whether it is a scattering, or a breaking up into atoms, or annihilation, it is either extinction or change.

33. On pain: pain that is unbearable takes us out of life; pain that lasts a long time can be borne. The mind keeps its own calm by withdrawing into itself, and the ruling faculty is not made worse. As for the parts that are harmed by the pain, let them, if they can, give their own opinion of it.

34. On fame: look at the minds of those who seek it—what they are like, what sort of things they avoid, and what sort of things they pursue. And consider this: just as heaps of sand, piled one on another, bury the sand that was there before, so in life what comes first is soon covered by what comes after.

35. From Plato: "Take a man of lofty mind, who surveys all time and all that exists. Do you suppose he can think that human life is anything great?" "It is not possible," he said. "Then such a man will not think that death is anything bad either." "Certainly not."
36. From Antisthenes: It is kingly to do good and to be badly spoken of.
37. It is shameful for the face to obey the mind, arranging and composing itself as the mind commands, while the mind is not arranged and composed by itself.
38. We should not be angry at things; for they do not care at all.
39. Give joy to the immortal gods and to us.
40. Life must be harvested like ripe ears of grain: one person is born, another dies.
41. If the gods do not care for me and my children, there is a reason for this.
42. For the good is on my side, and the just.
43. No joining others in their wailing, no violent emotion.

44. From Plato: "But I would give this man a fair answer, and it is this: You are wrong if you think that someone who is good for anything at all should weigh up the risk of living or dying. He should rather look to this alone in everything he does: whether he is acting justly or unjustly, and doing the work of a good person or a bad one."

45. "For this is the truth of it, men of Athens: wherever someone has taken his post because he thought it the best place for him, or has been posted there by a commander, there, in my opinion, he ought to stay and face the danger. He should put nothing ahead of the shame of deserting his post—neither death nor anything else."

46. "But, my good friend, consider whether what is noble and good is not something other than saving and being saved. As for living this long or that long, at least for one who is truly a man, consider whether this is not something to put out of his thoughts. He must not be in love with life. He must leave these matters to God and believe what the women say, that no one can escape his destiny; and then the next question is how he may best live the time he has to live."
47. Watch the courses of the stars as though you were running along with them; and keep thinking about how the elements change into one another. Such thoughts wash away the filth of life on earth.

48. This is a fine saying of Plato: whoever is talking about human beings should also look at earthly things as if from some high place above them. He should look at them in their gatherings, armies, work in the fields, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, the noise of the law courts, deserted places, all the various barbarian nations, festivals, mourning, markets: a mixture of everything, and an ordered combination of opposites.

49. Look at the past—so many great changes in who holds power. From it you can foresee what is to come as well. For it will certainly have the same form; it cannot break away from the order of what happens now. So to have watched human life for forty years is the same as to have watched it for ten thousand years. For what more will you see?

50. What has grown from the earth returns to the earth; but what has sprung from heavenly seed goes back to the heavenly realms. This is either the breaking up of the atoms' entanglement with one another, or some similar scattering of the elements that have no feeling.
51. With food and drink and cunning magic, turning the stream's course aside to escape from death. The wind that heaven sends we must endure, and toil on without complaining.

52. Another person may be better at throwing his opponent in wrestling; but he is not more devoted to the common good, nor more modest, nor better trained to meet whatever happens, nor more understanding of his neighbors' faults.

53. Wherever a task can be done in keeping with the reason that gods and human beings share, there is nothing to fear. For where we can gain benefit through activity that goes well and follows the way we are made, no harm need be suspected.

54. Everywhere and always, it is in your power to accept your present situation with reverence, to deal justly with the people around you, and to work skillfully on the thoughts you have now, so that nothing slips into them without being properly examined.

55. Do not look around to find out what other people's ruling faculties are like. Look straight at this: where is nature leading you? Both the nature of the universe, through what happens to you, and your own nature, through what you must do. Every being ought to do what follows from its constitution. And all other things have been made for the sake of rational beings—just as, among things without reason, the lower exist for the sake of the higher—but rational beings have been made for the sake of one another. The first principle in a human being's constitution, then, is that it is made for community. The second is not to give in to the persuasions of the body. For it is the special work of rational and intelligent activity to keep within its own limits, and never to be overpowered by the stirrings of the senses or of the appetites, since both of these are animal. The activity of intelligence claims to be in charge, and does not let itself be overpowered by the others. And rightly so, for nature made it to make use of all of them. The third thing in the rational constitution is freedom from error and from being deceived. So let the ruling faculty hold fast to these things and go straight on its way; then it has what is its own.
56. Think of yourself as dead, as having finished your life up to this moment; and live the rest that is granted to you in keeping with nature.
57. Love only what happens to you, what is spun for you with the thread of your destiny. For what could suit you better?

58. In everything that happens, keep before your eyes those to whom the same things happened: how they resented them, treated them as strange, and found fault with them. And where are they now? Nowhere. Why, then, do you want to act the same way? Why not leave these agitations, which are foreign to nature, to those who stir them up and those who are stirred by them? Why not devote yourself entirely to making the right use of what happens to you? For then you will use it well, and it will be material for you to work on. Only pay attention to yourself, and resolve to be a good person in every act you do. And remember…
59. Look within. Within is the spring of good, and it will keep welling up, if you keep digging.

60. The body, too, should be firmly set, and show no disorder in its movement or its posture. What the mind achieves in the face, by keeping it intelligent and composed, should be required of the whole body as well. But all this should be done without putting on a show.
61. The art of living is more like the wrestler's art than the dancer's, in this respect: it must stand ready and firm to meet blows that come suddenly and without warning.

62. Keep observing who the people are whose approval you want, and what their ruling faculties are like. Then you will neither blame those who do wrong without meaning to, nor want their approval, if you look at the sources of their opinions and desires.

63. "Every soul," the philosopher says, "is deprived of truth against its will." So, in the same way, it is deprived of justice, self-control, kindness and everything of that kind against its will. It is most necessary to keep this constantly in mind, for it will make you gentler toward everyone.

64. Whenever you are in pain, have this thought ready: there is nothing shameful in it, and it does not make the mind that governs you worse. For pain does not damage that mind, either as far as it is rational or as far as it is made for community. In most pains, let this saying of Epicurus help you: pain is neither unbearable nor endless, if you remember that it has its limits and if you add nothing to it in your imagination. And remember this too: we do not notice that many things we find unpleasant are really the same as pain—such as heavy drowsiness, being scorched by heat, and having no appetite. So when you are discontented about any of these things, tell yourself that you are giving in to pain.
65. Take care that you do not feel toward inhuman people as they feel toward human beings.

66. How do we know that Telauges was not better in character than Socrates? It is not enough that Socrates died a nobler death, and argued more skillfully with the sophists, and endured a night in the cold with more toughness; that when he was ordered to arrest Leon of Salamis he thought it nobler to refuse; and that he swaggered through the streets—though one may well doubt whether that was true. What we ought to ask is what kind of soul Socrates had. Was he able to be content with being just toward people and reverent toward the gods? Was he neither pointlessly resentful of people's wickedness, nor making himself a slave to anyone's ignorance? Did he neither receive anything that fell to his share from the whole as something strange, nor endure it as unbearable? And did he keep his mind from sharing in the feelings of the wretched flesh?

67. Nature has not mixed the mind so closely with the body that it has left you no power to draw a boundary around yourself and keep under your own control everything that is your own. For it is very possible to be a godlike person and be recognized as such by no one. Always keep this in mind; and this too: that very little indeed is needed to live a happy life. And just because you have given up hope of becoming a skilled logician or an expert in the study of nature, do not on that account give up hope of being free and modest, made for community and obedient to God.

68. It is in your power to live free from all compulsion, in the greatest peace of mind, even if the whole world shouts against you as much as it likes, and even if wild beasts tear apart the limbs of this kneaded lump of matter that has grown around you. For in the middle of all this, what prevents the mind from keeping its calm, from judging rightly everything around it, and from being ready to use whatever is put in front of it? Then judgment can say to whatever comes before it: "This is what you really are, even if people think you look like something else." And use can say to whatever comes to hand: "You are just what I was looking for." For to me, whatever presents itself is always material for virtue, the virtue of a rational being and a citizen—in a word, material for exercising the skill that belongs to a human being or to God. For everything that happens is related either to God or to a human being; it is neither new nor hard to handle, but familiar and ready material to work on.
69. Perfection of character means this: to live each day as if it were your last, without frantic agitation, without sluggishness, and without putting on an act.

70. The gods, who are immortal, do not resent having to put up, for so long, with people such as they are, so many of them bad; and more than that, they take care of them in every way. But you, who will so soon come to an end, are you tired of putting up with the bad—and that when you are one of them yourself?
71. It is absurd for a person not to escape from his own badness, which is actually possible, but to try to escape from other people's badness, which is impossible.
72. Whatever the faculty that is rational and made for community finds to be neither intelligent nor made for community, it rightly judges to be beneath itself.
73. When you have done a good deed and someone else has received it, why do you still look for a third thing besides these, as fools do—to be known for having done good, or to get something back?
74. No one gets tired of receiving what is useful. And acting in keeping with nature is useful. So do not get tired of receiving what is useful by doing it for others.

75. The nature of the whole set out to make the universe. So now, either everything that happens follows as a consequence of that, in an unbroken chain; or even the most important things, toward which the ruling power of the universe directs its own impulse, are governed by no rational principle. If you remember this, it will make you calmer about many things.
